vignette: Thomas had spent most of his life in the quiet rhythm of a civil service office, answering letters, filing reports, and rarely finding himself alone in a room with a man. The trauma that shattered that rhythm began one autumn evening when his long-time partner, a woman with a volatile temper, grabbed him by the arm and slammed him against the kitchen wall. The physical force left bruises that darkened the inside of his ribs, and the emotional pain left a deep sense of helplessness. In that instant, Thomas felt a loss of control that would echo in every corridor of his future days. The sound of his partner's voice, the smell of sweat, the taste of metallic blood-these sensations were seared into his mind in a single, terrifying flash. The loss of control he felt during that night became the first trigger that pulled Thomas into a defensive loop. Whenever he sensed a male presence in a closed space-be it a conference room or a narrow hallway-his mind rushed to the memory of being overpowered. This trigger drove him to adopt a constant socializing strategy: he would fill his day with brief conversations, small tasks, and the presence of other people so that he was never alone with his thoughts. At the same time, Thomas detaches from the memory itself, telling himself he is "too tired to think about it" whenever the recollection threatens to surface. By keeping people around him, he hopes the familiarity of voices will stave off the feeling of helplessness, but the effort to remain in a crowd also creates a sense that he is always on guard, further entrenching his perception of loss of control. The triggers also sharpened the memory itself. The next morning, as he walked through the office stairwell, the echo of the partner's harsh whisper made his ears flood with a taste he could still feel-an iron tang that clung to his tongue. When he stared at the black ink on a page, the scene unfolded behind his eyes like a photographic snapshot: the kitchen, the walls, the motion of his hands. These vivid images came with such clarity that they made it difficult for Thomas to deliberately recall the event. The more he tried to pull the memory into conscious thought, the harder it became, and the more it seemed to dissolve into a distant, almost dream-like image. When the memory surfaced in this vivid, almost automatic way, it in turn re-ignited the same triggers. The taste of blood that flooded his mouth whenever he imagined the attack turned the otherwise ordinary fluorescent lighting of the office into a threatening glare. Even the hum of the copy machine seemed to echo the hiss of a knife. Each time the memory returned, Thomas's fear of a male presence sharpened, and his belief that he had lost control resurfaced, setting the stage for his next defensive maneuver. Detaching from the memory, his most frequent maladaptive strategy, fed back into the memory in a subtle but powerful way. Because Thomas habitually told himself to "move on," he had become skilled at pulling the memory out of conscious recall. Yet, in moments of forced social interaction-when he was forced to talk to a colleague about a project-his mind would leap to the event, as if the conversation served as a cue for the memory to reappear. The constant need to be surrounded by people, combined with the deliberate avoidance of being alone, made it almost impossible for him to process the memory in a healthy, reflective way. The strategies themselves became triggers. The more Thomas kept himself surrounded, the more he felt a sense of alienation, as if he were living in a cage of people who could not understand his terror. The constant socializing created a pressure to conform, making him feel as though he had no control over his own narrative. Detaching from the memory made him feel out of sync with his own life; he could not explain to anyone why he was so uneasy around men in a single office. These feelings of detachment and alienation fed back into his perception of loss of control, forming a reinforcing loop that tightened with each passing day. In the present, Thomas is a civil servant who often finds himself in meetings with senior male officers. He has begun to avoid conference rooms by arriving late or leaving early, which has caused colleagues to question his reliability. His constant need to be in the presence of others has begun to impair his performance: deadlines slip because he spends too much time on small talk, and the memory of the abuse flares when he hears a man's voice in a quiet hallway. The cycle has grown tighter, and the isolation that once kept him safe now feels like a threat. Thomas has finally decided to seek help because he fears that, if he does not break this pattern, he will lose his job and the only steady anchor he has left. What he hopes most is to learn a way to face the male presence in the office without the flood of vivid taste and photographic recall, and to regain a sense of control that has eluded him since that night.
